reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Caused by activating (gain-of-function) mutations in GLUD1 encoding glutamate dehydrogenase, usually dominant and often de novo
Combines congenital hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia with persistent, usually mild, asymptomatic hyperammonaemia that does not fluctuate with feeds
Hypoglycaemia is characteristically protein-sensitive, triggered by leucine-rich meals, so both fasting and post-protein hypoglycaemia occur
The hyperammonaemia is typically not associated with the encephalopathy, protein aversion or precipitants seen in urea cycle defects
Hypoglycaemia is hyperinsulinaemic and hypoketotic, with inappropriately suppressed ketones and fatty acids and a glycaemic response to glucagon
Management combines measures for hyperinsulinism (including diazoxide-type therapy) with avoidance of large leucine/protein loads and provision of glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia
There is an increased risk of seizures and neurodevelopmental problems, partly independent of hypoglycaemia, so early recognition and monitoring matter
reference.pathophysiology: Glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH), encoded by GLUD1, catalyses oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and ammonia in the mitochondrion and is allosterically regulated, being inhibited by GTP and activated by leucine. Gain-of-function mutations reduce GTP inhibition, leaving GDH overactive. In pancreatic beta cells this raises the ratio of ATP generation and triggers inappropriate insulin secretion, especially after a leucine (protein) load, producing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia. In the liver and elsewhere, increased GDH activity raises ammonia production, giving a persistent hyperammonaemia. The excess ammonia usually remains modest and does not cause the classic urea cycle encephalopathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic congenital hyperinsulinism (e.g. KATP-channel defects)
Fatty-acid oxidation disorders with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
Transient neonatal hyperinsulinism (infant of a diabetic mother, perinatal stress)
additionalInvestigations: Critical (hypoglycaemia) sample showing detectable insulin with suppressed ketones and free fatty acids
Plasma ammonia demonstrating persistent mild-to-moderate elevation
Glucagon stimulation test showing a glycaemic response consistent with hyperinsulinism
Protein/leucine tolerance assessment demonstrating protein-sensitive hypoglycaemia
GLUD1 molecular genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis
Plasma amino acids and urine organic acids to exclude urea cycle and organic acid disorders
redFlags: Recurrent hypoglycaemic seizures or reduced consciousness in infancy
Persistent hyperammonaemia without an alternative explanation
Neurodevelopmental delay or epilepsy despite glycaemic control
reference.prognosis: With treatment of the hyperinsulinism and avoidance of large protein loads, hypoglycaemia is often manageable and the hyperammonaemia is generally benign; however, there remains an elevated risk of epilepsy and neurodevelopmental difficulties that may not be fully explained by hypoglycaemia alone.
pitfalls: Mistaking the hyperammonaemia for a urea cycle disorder and instituting inappropriate protein restriction protocols
Overlooking protein sensitivity by testing only fasting tolerance
Attributing hypoglycaemia to something other than hyperinsulinism because ketones are inappropriately low
Assuming good glycaemic control removes all neurodevelopmental and seizure risk
references: Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
